 Print this Article 
 View Comments “Secrets” by Bob Woodward. Lisa Berg/Simon & Schuster The most famous reporter in Washington approaches, armed with meeting notes, diary entries, two Pulitzer Prizes, and a reputation for protecting his sources. He already knows so much — perhaps too much. And now he is a supplicant. “I need your help,” he says. 
 Who could resist such a seduction? 
 Not many, it turns out. In “ Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir ,” Bob Woodward, 83, finally outs an array (though not all) of his confidential sources. He also lifts the veil on his reporting methods, which rely on his unique combination of Midwestern charm, chutzpah, extraordinary meticulousness, and a work ethic that has served him well since before his Watergate days. He counsels “taking people as seriously as they take themselves” and being “calm, unflappable, but aggressively persistent.” 
 Related : From Bob Woodward to Dianna Russini, the danger of getting too close to a source “Secrets” is a curious amalgam, engrossing almost in spite of itself. It combines disclosures about Woodward’s sourcing with passages culled from many of his previous 23 books, along with tidbits about his life and career. 
 Get Starting Point A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday. Enter Email Sign Up For “ The Brethren ” (1979), for example, he and his coauthor, Scott Armstrong, interviewed an astonishing 170 law clerks and five sitting US Supreme Court justices. He names all five now, for the first time, and says that one — Justice Potter Stewart — later complained to him that his inside look at the Supreme Court contained “too much truth.” 
 No one comes to Woodward’s books for stylish prose or self-revelation. “Secrets” makes no claim to literary elegance. And though he calls it “a project in self-discovery,” the emphasis is on his journalistic coups. 
 One exception is his suggestion that childhood anxiety over his parents’ crumbling marriage inspired his passion for unearthing secrets. “You have to snoop,” he concluded after finding a letter about their divorce. For the most part, though, the inner Woodward stays concealed, an elusive investigative quarry even for the man himself. 
 Related : Bob Woodward to Boston University graduates: ‘Don’t be afraid to try new things’ Hints of character do emerge. Undeterred by a failed tryout, Woodward badgers his way back to The Washington Post after just a year on a Maryland weekly. As a night police reporter, Woodward showed up mornings, too, working an uncompensated day shift — to the dismay of the newspaper union. The assiduousness is a lifelong habit. He types a memo after every interview, retains nearly every scrap of paper, and can tell you how many times he has spoken to each source. He is obsessive, perhaps to a fault. 
 A former US Navy officer and Yale graduate who grew to hate the Vietnam War , Woodward has worried for decades about the security of the country’s nuclear arsenal and still does. He cultivates sources at all levels of government, from US presidents to secretaries and bodyguards. A friendly security guard allowed him into the hospital room where he secured that controversial Iran-Contra scandal confession, reported in “ Veil ” (1987), from CIA director William J. Casey, another longtime confidante. 
 Woodward’s most famous source was, of course, Mark Felt, deputy director of the FBI and Watergate’s Deep Throat . The two met years earlier in a White House waiting room when Woodward, not yet a reporter, was still working at the Pentagon. “I turned the empty time into a career-counseling session,” Woodward recalls, and afterward he called Felt regularly for advice. By the time Watergate broke, they were close. An ailing Felt outed himself as Deep Throat in a 2005 Vanity Fair article. 
 In “Secrets,” Woodward adds that two of Nixon’s own defense lawyers, Fred Buzhardt and Leonard Garment, disliked their client enough to leak incriminating information to the reporter investigating him. 
 Related : 10 things to know from Bob Woodward’s new Trump book Woodward has named sources, he says, only if at least one of three conditions was met: Either the people in question were dead, they were already “readily identifiable” from the public record, or they gave specific permission. The unstated presumption is that Woodward makes clear to sources that confidentiality expires when they die. When one interviewee demanded even posthumous anonymity, Woodward says it was “the first time” anyone had made such a request. 
 Among modern US presidents, only Richard Nixon, Ronald Reagan, and George H.W. Bush snubbed Woodward. Donald Trump invited the reporter into the Oval Office but later sued him unsuccessfully for publishing tapes of their conversations. 
 Hillary Clinton was a “secret source,” as were dozens of Cabinet members and other government officials. Among them were former secretary of state and national security adviser Henry Kissinger, Air Force Major General Brent Scowcroft (Kissinger’s deputy and successor), Secretary of State Colin Powell (“a dear friend” with “the potential to be a great president”), and Senator Lindsay Graham , a South Carolina Republican. 
 Woodward describes Richard G. Darman, a key economic adviser in both the Reagan and George H.W. Bush administrations, as both his “best friend” and an invaluable source. The potential conflict of interest exploded when Woodward chose to publish stories on infighting over Bush economic policies in The Washington Post before the 1992 election. Darman had believed the details he spilled were destined only for an eventual book, and the two men never repaired their rupture. 
 Related : ‘Worry of a coup’: Revelations from Bob Woodward’s new book ‘Peril’ about the transition from the Trump to Biden administration There were other disappointments in what Woodward calls an “incredibly fortunate” life. As the Post’s metropolitan editor, he oversaw Janet Cooke’s fabricated, Pulitzer Prize-winning 1980 story about an 8-year-old heroin addict. That mistake ensured that he would never run the newspaper. Now, from his mostly honorary perch as associate editor, he calls out Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos, whom he previously admired, for “directly compromising public trust” in its journalism. 
 Woodward alludes to personal failures, too: a pair of unsuccessful marriages before a long, happy union with Elsa Walsh, a fellow reporter who (at least) once surrendered a scoop to him. Woodward already had demonstrated his love by entrusting her with his most precious secret: the identity of Deep Throat. 
 Julia M. Klein, a cultural reporter and critic in Philadelphia, has been a three-time finalist for the National Book Critics Circle’s Nona Balakian Citation for Excellence in Reviewing. 
 Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir 
 By Bob Woodward with Claire McMullen 
 Simon & Schuster, 592 pages, $35
